lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- Cut It in Half
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Joyce Michalczuk | Lesson 3 -- Cut It in Half

listenings.text: I sit on the leadership team of a logistics company, and I read about two hundred emails a day. Here is my rule. If you cannot give me your point in thirty seconds, you do not have a point yet. You have a topic. The people who move up in this company are not the ones who know the most. They are the ones who can cut. Last week a manager in Brazil sent me a four-page update. I read the first paragraph and I called her. I said, tell me the headline. She said it in one sentence, and it was a good sentence. So why was it on page three? Say the headline first. If I want the details, I will ask for them, and I usually do not.

I train new managers, and I hear the thirty-second rule all the time. I think it is dangerous. Short is not the same as clear. When you cut too much, you cut the one sentence of context that makes the number make sense, and then the director decides something wrong, very quickly. I have seen it happen twice this year. So my advice is different. Keep it short, yes, but keep one sentence of why. The headline, one reason, and what you need. That is not thirty seconds. That is forty-five. The extra fifteen seconds are the cheapest insurance in the company.
